<reflection>
The second experiment (low catalyst concentration) successfully differentiated some mechanisms, with M16, M11, M14, and M20 emerging as the best fits. However, many mechanisms still have very similar negative log-likelihood values, indicating that the data so far is not sufficient to uniquely identify the mechanism. The aim of probing catalyst concentration dependence was achieved, but further discrimination is needed. We now need an experiment that can break the degeneracy among the top candidates and other plausible mechanisms.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
Introducing initial product will test for reversibility and product-induced effects. Many mechanisms include a reversible product binding step (e.g., M1, M2, etc.), which would lead to a slower net forward rate due to the reverse reaction. Mechanisms with product-induced inactivation (M12, M17) would show enhanced inactivation, altering the time profile. Mechanisms without product interactions would be unaffected. This experiment is effective because it adds a new dimension (product concentration) that differentially affects a broad range of candidate mechanisms, helping to distinguish between reversible and irreversible models, as well as product-sensitive and product-insensitive inactivation pathways. By using the same substrate and catalyst concentrations as the first experiment but with added product, we can directly compare the kinetics with and without product, maximizing interpretability.
</hypothesis>
